nameStory: The Arctic Tern gets its name from its incredible journey to the Arctic regions where it breeds each summer. These amazing birds nest as far north as the Arctic Circle, making them true citizens of the polar world during breeding season.
description: Arctic Terns are graceful, medium-sized seabirds that look like elegant white gulls with sleek, pointed wings. They measure about 11-15 inches long with a wingspan of 26-30 inches, roughly the size of a small gull. During breeding season, they sport a distinctive black cap, bright red-orange bill and legs, and a deeply forked tail that gives them their characteristic swallow-like silhouette in flight.

idTips.label: Blood-red bill and legs
idTips.description: In breeding plumage, the bill and legs are a striking bright red-orange color that looks almost like it was dipped in paint—much more vivid than the darker bills of other terns

idTips.label: Deeply forked tail
idTips.description: The tail splits into two long, pointed streamers that trail behind in flight, creating a distinctive swallow-like profile that's more pronounced than other terns

idTips.label: Complete black cap
idTips.description: During breeding season, the entire top of the head from bill to nape is jet black, contrasting sharply with bright white cheeks and throat

idTips.label: Narrow black wing tips
idTips.description: In flight, look for thin dark trailing edges on the wing tips that create a subtle but distinctive border against the otherwise pale gray and white wings

idTips.label: Aggressive diving behavior
idTips.description: Watch for their spectacular fishing technique—they hover 30-50 feet above water before plunging straight down with wings folded back in a dramatic splash

habitat: Arctic Terns are found along New England's rocky coastlines, barrier beaches, and offshore islands during migration and occasionally breeding. They prefer isolated sandy or pebbly areas near cold, fish-rich waters, especially around places like the rocky shores of Maine or Massachusetts' outer islands. Look for them diving for small fish in coastal waters, particularly where currents bring nutrients close to shore.

seasonality.spring: Arctic Terns arrive in late April to May in full breeding plumage with bright red bills and complete black caps, often seen in small flocks along the coast.
seasonality.summer: Peak breeding season finds them at their most vibrant, with brilliant red-orange bills and legs. They're actively fishing and may be seen with their distinctive hovering and diving behavior.
seasonality.fall: Migration begins in August-September as birds start to molt. Bills and legs fade to black, and the black cap becomes mottled with white on the forehead.
seasonality.winter: Most Arctic Terns have departed for their incredible journey south, though rare stragglers may appear with winter plumage showing black bills and partial white foreheads.

funFact: Arctic Terns make the longest migration of any animal on Earth—some individuals fly up to 60,000 miles per year, essentially seeing two summers as they travel from Arctic breeding grounds to Antarctic waters and back, experiencing more daylight than any other creature on the planet.
confusionNotes: Arctic Terns are most easily confused with Common Terns, but remember 'Red for Arctic'—Arctic Terns have bright red-orange bills in breeding season while Common Terns have orange bills with black tips. Arctic Terns also have shorter legs and a more deeply forked tail.
compareHints: Among New England's terns, Arctic Terns are distinguished from Common Terns by their solid red bills (no black tip) and more deeply forked tails. Compared to Roseate Terns, Arctic Terns have grayer wings and lack the pinkish breast tinge that Roseates show in breeding plumage. Forster's Terns have orange legs year-round and different tail patterns, while Arctic Terns show bright red legs only in breeding season.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to other New England terns, Common Terns are the most likely to be seen inland on lakes and rivers, while Roseate Terns stick closer to saltwater and have longer, more deeply forked tails.
Compared to Common Terns, Roseates are more delicate with longer, more elegant proportions and that distinctive pink breast wash.
Forster's Tern differs from Common Tern most obviously in winter with its black eye mask versus the Common's black cap extending to the eye.
